data.name: The Blue Flamingo
data.detailed_description:
Pilots from all around the world are gathering to challenge each other on a danger-filled course. You are making the final preparations and your ship, The Blue Flamingo, is ready in the hangar.

About The Blue Flamingo:

Shoot your way through intense levels with swiftly increasing difficulty. Invest your score in upgrades or save your score to gain interest with the risk of losing it all.

This is a game that challenges you to reach the highest possible score, made interesting by an economical system that allows you to invest your score in upgrades, which makes earning more score points easier. But on the other hand, you are rewarded with interest on what is left of your score when you progress to the next level. Therefore, you must make a choice - upgrade and try to regain the score or rely on your skills to beat the increasingly difficult levels. Act wisely to beat your friends and climb up the score table.

Experience a bite-sized shoot 'em up game created entirely with handmade models. A 32-foot long handcrafted model was built for the game, along with countless props and assets that were filmed and photographed. All the effects, rocket flares and explosions were created with firecrackers and pyrotechnics.

reviews.review:
[h1]The Blue Flamingo — I'm recommending the craftsmanship, not the game[/h1]

[b]TL;DR: Thumbs up, but conditionally. The game itself is a very basic shmup. What earns the recommendation is how it was made.[/b]

[h2]This thing was built by hand, physically[/h2]

Might and Delight, a small studio out of Stockholm making games since 2010, didn't model this world — they built it. A roughly 32-foot (about 10 metre) handcrafted set was constructed specifically for the game, along with countless props and vehicles. All of it was then filmed and photographed, green-screened, and turned into sprites.

The vehicles were pulled along on strings and magnets. Every explosion and rocket flare in this game is an actual firecracker going off on a model set.

[b]That is the entire reason I'm giving this a thumbs up.[/b] In 2026, in the middle of the AI era, that kind of stubborn, physical, handmade work is genuinely rare, and it deserves applause. They didn't have the budget for something bigger back in 2014 — but they made something real, and I'd rather reward that today than pretend it doesn't count because it's twelve years old.

[i][Screenshot 1: the train running along the desert stretch in level 1][/i]
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3799542242

Look at that shot knowing it's a physical model. You can [i]see[/i] it. Somebody put serious work into that. Maybe it's just some sort of self-confirmation bias/self-fulfilling prophecy, but knowing how the game was made, you can see the props being physically made objects.

[h2]Now the honest part[/h2]

Without that context, this would be a thumbs down from me. Let me be clear about why.

[b]1. I'm not the audience for this kind of shmup.[/b] I like bullet hell. Old-school Galaga / Space Invaders-style vertical shooters are just not my thing. That's a taste issue, not a flaw.

[b]2. The loop is very thin.[/b] It's an endless stream of broadly similar enemies, and your only two upgrade paths are more/better weapons and more bombs. That's it. As an upgrade system it's about as simple as it gets.

[b]3. €10 is a lot.[/b] I have to say it plainly: in 2026 we're used to this level of polish and far beyond it, because it's become so much easier to produce. Ten euros for this feels disproportionate on pure content-per-euro terms — even though I fully understand that the handmade production is exactly what you're paying for.

[h2]A bug in level 2[/h2]

From level 2 onwards my screen turned into an old TV "no signal" error display. Points for style — using a retro TV fault screen instead of just going black is genuinely funny — but it's not a good sign that the second level broke immediately.

I don't know whether this is specific to my setup, specific to Steam Deck, or general. Either way it made the level effectively unplayable.

[i][Screenshot 2: the TV error screen in level 2][/i]
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3799542669

[h2]Steam Deck: not optimised, but easily fixed[/h2]

Twelve years old, mixed reviews, basically nobody still playing it — no surprise it isn't Deck-optimised. But it's [b]absolutely playable[/b], and the fix takes about twenty seconds:

In the Steam controller settings, switch the layout template to [b]"Keyboard (WASD) and Mouse"[/b]. The game's own default setup does not work at all. With the template swapped, nothing else needs configuring.

From there it plays fine:
[list]
[*] RT to shoot, LT for bombs
[*] Left stick to move your ship
[*] Right stick, gyro, touchpad or touchscreen for anything you need to click
[/list]

Honestly, calling this a major criticism would be overstating it. It's a twenty-second fix and then it just works.

[h2]Who this is actually for[/h2]

As a game demanding your full attention, it isn't interesting. As a [b]secondary activity[/b], it's surprisingly well suited.

If you listen to podcasts and need something visual running alongside to keep your head actually [i]on[/i] the podcast — I know that pattern well — this does the job nicely. Same if you just want to switch your brain off, think about life a bit, and have something moving on screen. It also works fine on a Deck on a train.

And it's a genuinely good deed at the same time, because you're putting money toward a small studio that did something remarkable.

[h2]Verdict[/h2]

[b]Recommended — with conditions.[/b] Buy it if you want a simple shmup for background play, or if you want to support real handcrafted indie work. Don't buy it expecting depth, and know that €10 is steep for what's mechanically here. But somebody built a ten-metre set and set off firecrackers to make this game, and I'm not going to give that a thumbs down.
